messages:
maya: Heads up — saw p95/p99 token latency regressions (~+1.0-1.2s) after we flipped on MIG + time-slicing for the embedding nodepool in us-west2. Happens during bursty embed traffic (~150-250 req/min). Anyone else see this? 😕

josh: Can you paste an `nvidia-smi` / `kubectl top pod` snapshot from the time? Also which nodepool name? Could be NIC / PCIe contention rather than GPU.

maya: quick dumps from spike window:
```
$ kubectl top pods -n inference | head
NAME                         CPU(cores)   MEMORY(bytes)
embedder-xyz-7f5d4         120m         420Mi
batcher-embed-12           80m          260Mi

$ nvidia-smi dmon -s u -o DT
#Gpu,Pid,Type,SM,Memory,Enc,Dec
0,    -,     -,   94,  1200Mi, -, -
# no single GPU at 100% — looks spread across MIG slices
```
also infra-bot posted an alert at the same time: "node/gpu-emb-3: enp1s0 rx drops 12% and tx drops 8%"

infra-bot: Alert: node/gpu-emb-3 -> enp1s0 rx drops > 10% (15:12 UTC), pods on node: embedder-xyz-7f5d4, batcher-embed-12

sophia: This smells like network/small-packet saturation. MIG/time-slicing increases #contexts hitting host and can blow up PCIe and NIC packet rates even if GPU utilization per slice is fine. On instance SKU X we already hit ENA queues with many small RPCs.

alex: Agreed. Two quick levers: 1) split by network throughput (high-bandwidth pool for heavy embedding) 2) prefer larger slices for steady throughput jobs. For bursty small embeddings we should avoid extra multiplexing.

josh: Also CA behaviour: our cluster-autoscaler only sees CPU/mem requests for those jobs (we advertise fractional GPU via device-plugin). CA scales wrong because it doesn't correlate slice count -> node capacity. We get scale-ups that place more pods on the same NIC.

sophia: Proposal: label nodepools with `node.k8s.redwood/gpu-net-class=high` vs `low`, and use `nodeAffinity` in the embedding deployment for highbw for batch-heavy routes. For small interactive routes use low-cost mig-timed nodes but cap concurrency with PodDisruptionBudget + concurrency limits.

maya: Example nodeSelector snippet we can roll out as an experiment:
```yaml
spec:
  template:
    spec:
      nodeSelector:
        node.k8s.redwood/gpu-net-class: "high"
      tolerations:
      - key: "gpu.slice"
        operator: "Exists"
```

josh: We should also teach autoscaler via a simple external metrics shim: emit `gpu.slice_utilization` (sum of active slices per node) and have an external-provisioner scale nodepool desired size based on that. Quick interim: increase `--scale-down-unneeded-time` so CA doesn't thrash and we keep warm capacity for spikes.

alex: Cost/benefit quick math (ballpark):
- HighBW nodes (8xA10G 100G NIC) ~ $X/hr -> supports 400 qps stable for embeddings
- Many MIG-sliced cheaper nodes -> saves 30% on GPU cost but needs additional high-bw nodes or warm pool to avoid latency spikes -> net saving shrinks to ~10% after adding warm high-bw reserve.

sophia: TL;DR: MIG+timeslice reduces GPU cost but increases host-level IO. For bursty small-request workloads we need either: (A) network-optimized nodepool for those workloads, (B) concurrency limits + batching, or (C) warm reserved nodes to absorb spikes.

maya: Action items:
- [ ] create `emb-highbw` nodepool (network optimized SKU) with label `gpu-net-class=high` (alex)
- [ ] patch embedder deployment to prefer `gpu-net-class=high` for /batch routes and keep interactive on current pool (maya)
- [ ] prototype external-metric exporter that counts active GPU slices per node (josh)
- [ ] run 48h A/B traffic test & capture p95/p99 + NIC drops (sophia)

josh: I'll spin up a PoC exporter and a small warm pool config in kops/terraform. If the 48h A/B confirms, we can iterate on pricing model and possibly add autoscaler hook for slice-metric.

maya: Thanks — ping me once `emb-highbw` is ready and I'll re-route a canary of 10% traffic. :thumbsup:
